note:
The book of Ezra deals with two sets of events, separated by more than half a century. In chs. 1–6, the focus is on the twenty-three years from the edict of Cyrus to the completion of the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem (538–515 B.C.), though two later incidents are mentioned in 4:6 and 4:7–23. The account is in two main sections: the return of the exiles (chs. 1; 2) and the rebuilding of the temple (chs. 3–6).

**1:1–4** By beginning with the decree of Cyrus, Ezra picks up the history of redemption where Chronicles leaves off. Verses 1–3 repeat, with minor differences, the closing words of 2 Chronicles.

**1:1 first year.** Beginning in 559 B.C., Cyrus ruled Anshan, a territory to the north of the Persian Gulf. He extended his rule over Medo-Persia around 550 B.C.., and, after conquering lands as far as Lydia in the west of Asia Minor, in October 539 his armies entered Babylon. The reference here is to 538 B.C. The spring of that year marked the start of the first year of his reign over his enlarged empire.

**that the word of the LORD ... might be fulfilled.** Jeremiah prophesied seventy years of captivity in Babylon (Jer. 25:11–12; 29:10; see Dan. 9:2) and also assured the exiles of the Lord’s plan for their future (Jer. 29:11). From 605, when the first captives were deported, to 538, when the decree to return was issued, is sixty-seven years. Other prophecies may also be in view (Jer. 16:14–15; 27:22). The Lord was sovereignly bringing to pass the word He had spoken more than half a century before.

**the LORD stirred up the spirit.** This phrase expresses the main theme of the book: God works sovereignly through responsible human agents to accomplish His redemptive plan (6:22; 7:27). In the words of Prov. 21:1, the Lord directed Cyrus’s spirit like “a stream of water ... he turns it wherever he will” (see Is. 41:25; 45:13).

Jewish advisors may have helped to write the decree.

**1:2 The** LORD**,** **the God of heaven.** A title identifying the Lord as the supreme authority and power, whose rule from on high was not constrained by any earthly boundary (5:12; 6:9, 10; 7:12, 21, 23; Neh. 1:4, 5; 2:4, 20; Dan. 2:18, 19, 37, 44; Jon. 1:9). “The God of heaven” was a divine title used by the Jews particularly in dealings with foreigners.

**has given me ... has charged me.** Cyrus’s testimony to the sovereignty of God is probably a diplomatic formality for him, since the famous Cylinder of Cyrus says similar things about other gods (1:3 note).

**a house at Jerusalem.** This “house” refers to the temple but in the end will include the city and the people of God. The rebuilding of the house of God is a dominant theme in Ezra and Nehemiah (see Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). Without the temple and its associated sacrifices, the spiritual needs of the community cannot be properly met.

Cyrus’s policy of religious toleration and support for the Jerusalem temple was similar to his treatment of other subject peoples. His purpose was to enlist the gods of these peoples in his own service (note the motivation of Darius in 6:10 and of Artaxerxes in 7:23). The Lord’s controlling purpose, however, was to continue the progress of his provision of salvation.

**of all his people.** Cyrus’s commission is directed to all the people, not the leaders, expressing a major theme of the book (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes): the people of God as a whole are vital to accomplishing God’s redemptive plan.

Refers to deported Jews of Cyrus’ era who have been compelled to live throughout the Babylonian Empire, and perhaps to Gentiles.

**be assisted.** In the exodus from Egypt, the Egyptians sent Israel out with gifts (Ex. 12:35, 36).

The response is described in language parallel to the decree, emphasizing the immediate reaction of the people to Cyrus’s decree and to God’s prompting (see Phil. 2:13).

**1:5 heads of the fathers’ houses.** The patriarchs of extended families.

**Judah and Benjamin.** The two southern tribes exiled by the Babylonians. There are also some survivors from the northern tribes, perhaps from those who had earlier moved south (see 1 Chr. 9:3; 2 Chr. 11:16).

**the priests and the Levites.** Restoration of the temple service requires their return (8:15–17).

**God had stirred.** The same Hebrew phrase as in v. 1. God’s sovereign power generates the decree and the response. Many Jews prefer to live under the conditions in their current location rather than face the challenges of returning to their ravaged homeland and the hardships entailed in rebuilding it, though they are willing to sponsor others.

verse_quote: aided them ... besides all that was freely offered.
note: Two sorts of donation are in view: the first is to assist the returnees; the freewill offerings are to support the temple.

There were three occasions on which the Babylonian king did this: in 605 B.C. (Dan. 1:2), in 597 B.C.. (2 Kin. 24:13), and in 586 B.C.. (2 Kin. 25:14–15). Cyrus returns them as a mark of respect for his subjects’ religion.

A Persian official named after Mithras, the sun god. “Treasurer” is also a Persian term.

**Sheshbazzar.** Identified by some as Zerubbabel. However, Sheshbazzar seems to be a somewhat unknown figure in 5:14–16, whereas Zerubbabel is well known (5:2, 3). Possibly Sheshbazzar is the official leader, perhaps a Persian designated by Cyrus, while Zerubbabel is the popular leader. More probably, Sheshbazzar, though appointed by the Persians, is himself a senior Jewish figure (see 2:63) who dies shortly after the return, leaving Zerubbabel, his second-in-command, in charge of the returnees.

**prince of Judah.** Not necessarily a connection with the line of David. It merely points to one who is a leader.

The total of the numbers in vv. 9, 10 is 2,499, not 5,400 as reported in v. 11. The reason for this discrepancy is not known, but the larger figure may include many smaller items not explicitly listed. The difficulty is compounded by not knowing exactly what the “basins” and “bowls” were. The production of these treasures must have encouraged the spirits of God’s people, since Jeremiah had prophesied that they would be preserved and carried back to Jerusalem (Jer. 27:22).

The exiles return to Jerusalem with the articles for the temple according to the decree of Cyrus. The Lord keeps His promise that after chastening His people for breaking the covenant, He would bring them back to the Promised Land (Deut. 30:1–5). Those who return are the legitimate successors of the pre-exilic community, and God is continuing to work for and through them.

This list of exiles who return may not appear theologically important, but the repetition of the same list, with some variations, in Neh. 7 suggests otherwise. First, the Lord knows His people personally. The covenant relation between the Lord and His people is a bond of intimate friendship. Second, common people are vital to the accomplishing of God’s redemptive plan (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). Not only the religious and political leaders but also the common people are important in rebuilding the house of God. In fact, “the rest of the people” contribute more to the rebuilding than do “the heads of the fathers’ houses” and the governor (Neh. 7:70–72). Third, the enumeration resembles that found in Numbers (1; 26) and Joshua (18; 19). As the Lord formed the covenant community after the exodus from Egypt, so He re-creates it after the return from Babylon. However, for the moment they remain “the people of the province” (v. 1), a subdivision of the vast Persian Empire. They have returned home, but they are still without political freedom.

His name means “offspring of Babylon,” a reference to his birth in exile. He is a descendant of David, the son of Shealtiel (3:2) and a grandson of King Jehoiachin (1 Chr. 3:17). The genealogy of Jesus is traced through him (Matt. 1:12, 13; Luke 3:27). He is probably recognized by the Persians as the civil leader of the restored community. He is responsible for laying the temple’s foundation (3:8–10).

**Jeshua.** As high priest at the time of the restoration (Hag. 1:1; Zech. 3:1), Jeshua, a variant spelling of Joshua, is the spiritual leader of the community. His grandfather Seraiah, high priest when Jerusalem fell to the Babylonians in 586 B.C., was executed at Rib­lah along with other notable citizens (2 Kin. 25:18–21; Jer. 52:24–27). However, Seraiah’s son Jehozadak was spared and taken to Babylon (1 Chr. 6:15), and now Jehozadak’s son has returned to Jerusalem.

**Nehemiah.** Not the same Nehemiah who later oversees the reconstruction of Jerusalem’s walls.

**Mordecai.** Not the same Mordecai who was Esther’s cousin.

**2:2–35** The first group listed is the laity. The list is in two parts: part one (vv. 3–20) gives the family names of the returnees, and part two (vv. 21–35) lists their towns in the tribal territories of Benjamin and Judah. The laity are mentioned ahead of the clergy in keeping with the emphasis in Ezra and Nehemiah on the significance of the common people in rebuilding the kingdom (2:1–70 note). The twelve leaders of the first return (see Neh. 7:7; only eleven are named here, as Nahamani is omitted) collectively represent the twelve tribes that make up the real Israel (see 6:17; 8:24, 35).

The next groups are officially associated with the temple service: priests (vv. 36–39), Levites (v. 40), singers (v. 41), gatekeepers (v. 42), temple servants (vv. 43–54), and Solomon’s servants (vv. 55–57). Solomon’s servants probably served in the temple, since they are counted together with the temple servants in v. 58.
The final group of returnees is made up of those who cannot prove their Israelite descent. Again, the laity is listed first (v. 60), then the priests (v. 61).
A man must be descended from Aaron in order to be a priest (Ex. 29:44; Num. 3:3).

Or _tirshatha_ (“his excellency”). Only Sheshbazzar has been given such status by Cyrus. What he says here strongly suggests that he is a Jew with a Babylonian name.

**the most holy food.** Only a priest or a member of his household could eat the portion of the sacrifice allotted to the priests (Lev. 22:10).

**Urim and Thummim.** A device for making decisions (Ex. 28:30), needed in this case to determine the ancestry of these priests, but neither the device nor the skill to use it have survived the exile.

The same total as in Neh. 7:66. However, the sum of the figures in the list in Ezra is only 29,818, while the sum of the list in Neh. 7 is 31,089. It may be that certain groups are being counted without being listed, or that an insignificant scribal copying mistake may have come into the text (see Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Special Issues).

The first temple was also built with freewill offerings (1 Chr. 29:1–9), not the tithe. The principle of giving beyond the tithe willingly and according to one’s ability is still at work in building the kingdom under the new covenant (2 Cor. 8:11).

Gold coins brought into use throughout the Persian Empire. The heavier “mina” (see text note) was a weight of silver, not a coin. In total, this verse refers to about 1,100 lbs. (500 kg) of gold and three tons (2,700 kg) of silver.

This final verse closes the section by echoing v. 1, in which they “came” and “returned”; in v. 70 they “lived in their towns.” The Lord has returned the people of promise to their ancestral homes in the Land of Promise.

The people rebuild the altar, resume the sacrifices (3:1–6), and then rebuild the temple itself (3:7–6:22). Spurred on by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah (5:1–2) and blessed by God (5:5), they succeed in spite of opposition from the peoples around them (ch. 4) and from the governor of “the province Beyond the River” (5:3–6:12).

**3:1–6** The exiles’ merely returning to Judah is insufficient. The worship of the Lord has to be resumed even though there is time only to build an altar at the site of the former temple.

**3:1 the seventh month.** Tishri (September–October), the month of the Feast of Booths (Lev. 23:33–44). The desire to celebrate this feast (3:4) no doubt provided the stimulus needed to rebuild the altar. The year is not stated. The decree permitting the Jews to return was issued in Cyrus’s first year, March 538–February 537 B.C., possibly in the summer (see 6:1, 2 note). After that, time was needed to organize the return, for the actual journey, and for an initial period of resettlement. In what follows the date 536 B.C. is assumed, but a case can be made for a year earlier or later.

**as one man.** The decision to reinstitute the worship of the Lord in proper form is unanimous.

The only place where Jeshua is mentioned first, as is appropriate for the priestly task of erecting the altar. Here and in v. 8, Sheshbazzar may have delegated Zerubbabel to represent him because of his belonging to the house of David (see 2:2; 5:14–16). It had been prophesied that one of David’s offspring would be involved in building the temple (2 Sam. 7:12, 13).

**burnt offerings.** Burnt offerings were the primary offerings (Lev. 1), but others are also in view (v. 5). The burnt offering was the continuing basis on which a sinful people could live in the presence of a holy God (Ex. 29:42), looking forward as it did to the sacrifice of Christ as the final sacrifice that brings sinners into the presence of God (Heb. 10:19–20).

**as it is written.** The written Word is a powerful tool used by God to accomplish His redemptive plan.

They have the courage to build the altar and lay the foundation of the temple. But their resolve will soon be tested (4:4, 5), and the work will stop (4:24).

**the peoples of the lands.** While some restrict this phrase to Judeans who never suffered exile (see 2 Kin. 25:12), it is more probably a reference to surrounding nations, including those groups settled by the Assyrians in the territory of the former kingdom of Israel to the north (see 2 Kin. 17:24).

Not only is the Feast of Booths celebrated from the fifteenth to the twenty-first of the month, but the entire sacrificial system is set in motion because the sacrifices are a part of maintaining the covenant relationship (Heb. 9:22). So important are the sacrifices that they are started before the temple itself is finished.

The workers are supervised by the Levites (v. 8), who are under the direction of the leading families in the community (v. 9).

**3:7** Steps are immediately taken to secure the craftsmen and materials to begin rebuilding the temple. The language of v. 7 recalls the materials assembled for Solomon’s temple (1 Chr. 22:2–4; 2 Chr. 2:8–16).

Ziv (or Iyar, April–May), the same time of year that Solomon began building the original temple (2 Chr. 3:2). Seven months have elapsed from 3:1 in procuring supplies. The year is probably 535 B.C.

**to supervise the work of the house of the** LORD**.** This phrasing is virtually identical to the language used about Solomon’s temple (1 Chr. 23:4).

verse_quote: when the builders laid the foundation.
note: The focus of the narrative is the response of the people rather than the mechanics of construction. If the return of the temple articles has encouraged the spirits of the people (1:9–11 note), much more does the laying of the foundation confirm their faith in God, who has promised restoration after exile (Deut. 30:1–5). Their expression of praise echoes exactly the dedication of Solomon’s temple (2 Chr. 5:13).

The tears of the older members of the community are not tears of joy but tears of disappointment because of the contrast between this small beginning (see Zech. 4:10) and the splendor of Solomon’s temple. Similar disappointment will later call for rebuke (Hag. 2:1–5), but for the moment the joy of the Lord is the strength of many.

News of what is happening in Jerusalem has spread quickly and attracted hostile attention. Work on the temple is delayed for more than a decade. The prophet Haggai also sheds light on events in this period, but he focuses on the reluctance of the people to continue rebuilding the temple in difficult economic circumstances. Ezra shows that their disinclination to proceed is also significantly influenced by external opposition. Indeed, in later years similar antagonism hampers attempts to refortify Jerusalem (vv. 6–23). Consequently, from here through to the end of Nehemiah the record is one of malice, harassment, and hostility. Whenever the cause of God moves forward, it encounters opposition.

**4:1 the adversaries.** Though these people come with outward expressions of good intentions, they are referred to as “adversaries,” since they are real­ly intent on undermining the work of restoration. Political factors play a part in this conflict. Only the returnees have authorization from Cyrus to undertake construction (1:2–4), and the leaders in Judah may be reluctant to accept the assistance of unauthorized persons lest the Judahites get into trouble with the empire. Ultimately, however, the trouble is religious. The adversaries include people from various places who were transplanted into Samaria, the area north of Judah, after the destruction of the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 B.C. (4:9, 10 note). They worship many gods and incorporate worship of the Lord into their polytheism (2 Kin. 17:24–41). The animosity between the Jews and the Samaritans who descend from these adversaries continues into the NT era (see John 4:1–42).

The incident that led to this is described in 2 Kin. 17:24–28, but the polytheism practiced by the peoples in Samaria does not warrant them adding “as you do” (cf. 2 Kin. 17:29–41).

**Esarhaddon.** Assyrian policy involved substantial resettlement of subject peoples. In addition to the influx after the fall of Samaria (see 3:3) and at a later period (see v. 10), there were also settlements in the north under Esarhaddon (681–669 B.C.).

The discrimination is not racial or political but religious. From the early days of living in the Promised Land (Judg. 3:6) and throughout their history (2 Kin. 17:7–17), the Israelites made alliances with foreigners that led them into idolatry and ultimately to exile from the land (2 Kin. 17:18–23). The failure of the returnees to separate themselves from the indigenous population became a problem before long (Ezra 9; 10). The same principle of religious separation is still operative under the new covenant (2 Cor. 6:14–7:1).

The “adversaries” of v. 1 (see 3:3).

**discouraged ... made them afraid.** The word “discouraged” is lit. “made hands limp” (see Neh. 6:9). These verbs are participles, indicating that this behavior extends over a considerable period of time.
Perhaps these are Persian officials. The obstructive efforts of the adversaries cause a delay in the work from the time of Cyrus (550–530 B.C..) until the second year of Darius (522–486 B.C..).

This material is a separate section, describing later opposition to the Jews during the reigns of Xerxes (486–465 B.C..) and Artaxerxes I (465–424 B.C..). The narrative justifies calling the neighboring peoples in v. 1 “adversaries.” Additionally, it shows that the opposition is not a brief and passing problem but a foretaste of prolonged opposition—to the people of God in rebuilding God’s ‘‘house” (the temple) and to the city and the nation in general.

**4:6 Ahasuerus.** Ahasuerus (Xerxes) succeeded Darius and was king of Persia from 486 to 465 B.C.

**they wrote an accusation.** The subject of the verb is not specified, but the context shows that the troublemakers are a later generation of the “adversaries” of v. 1. Nothing is said about the nature of the accusation.

Artaxerxes I, successor to Ahasuerus (Xerxes) and king of Persia from 465 to 424 B.C..

**wrote to Artaxerxes.** There is no information about the content of this letter, but considering the context, it is doubtless an effort to prevent rebuilding the wall.

**Aramaic.** The language of international diplomacy in the ancient Near East.

This section is written not in Hebrew but in Aramaic, the language of the original documents cited in this section. The correspondence expresses the concern of various Gentile officials about the progress of the Jews’ work.

**4:8 scribe.** Scribes are high officials who write official correspondence and keep archival records for the provincial government (7:6 note).
The opposition does not come from a few but is broadly based.

Probably Ashurbanipal, the last successful king of Assyria (668–627 B.C..), who transplanted various peoples into Samaria. This practice began after the fall of Samaria in 722 B.C., probably under Sargon II (2 Kin. 17:24).

**Beyond the River.** An extensive area west of the Euphrates, including Aram, Phoenicia, and Palestine.

This term came into common use after the exile because the majority of the returnees were from the tribe of Judah.

**from you.** “From you” (singular) refers to Artaxer­xes and may point to the group who returned with Ezra.

**finishing the walls.** See note on 4:6–23. The reference is to the walls and foundations of the city, not the temple.
The complainants cloak their motives by expressing concern for the revenues of the Persian Empire. They predict that if Jerusalem is walled, it will again rebel and cease paying taxes.

verse_quote: we eat the salt of the palace.
note: Lit. “we have salted with the salt of the palace.” Probably a way of referring to the covenantal obligation of a vassal to his overlord (see Lev. 2:13; Num. 18:19; 2 Chr. 13:5).

The various Aramaic documents used in writing this section of Ezra would be kept in a similar archive.

**a rebellious city ... was laid waste.** See 2 Kin. 18:7; 24:1.

Obviously an exaggeration, these words are intended to sway Artaxer­xes. This letter is written at a time when there is great unrest in the western provinces of the empire. The implied threat is probably that rebellion in Jerusalem will tip the balance of power in favor of those who oppose Persia.
The king is not given a summary of the letter; it is read to him word for word, probably translated from Aramaic into Persian.

Israel received tribute from other nations under David and Solomon. Now, even though they have returned to the Land of Promise, God’s people must submit to the rule of the ungodly (9:9 and note). The initial phase of the restoration is less than what the prophets expected (e.g., Isa. 60:1–3; Mic. 4:1–5), leaving the full restoration of God’s people in the hands of the Messiah, Jesus Christ.

verse_quote: that this city be not rebuilt.
note:
It is probable that the destruction of these newly built walls (“by force and power,” v. 23) is the subject of the report that Nehemiah receives in Neh. 1:3.

**until a decree is made by me.** The complainants do not get all they want. The possibility of Jerusalem’s walls being rebuilt is not entirely ruled out, but it is dependent on future imperial policy. Such a decree to rebuild the walls is made by Artaxerxes when he gives permission to Nehemiah to return and perform the work (Neh. 2:1–9).

After the section dealing with opposition to the rebuilding of the wall (vv. 6–23), the author returns to the topic of vv. 1–5, rebuilding the temple. The author uses a technique called “repetitive resumption,” in which the substance of vv. 4, 5 is repeated, not to add new information but to mark vv. 6–23 as a digression.

**the second year ... of Darius.** April 520 B.C.

In the same year referred to in 4:24, the second year of Darius, Haggai begins to prophesy in August (Hag. 1:1). Three weeks later, work resumes at the temple site, and Zechariah’s ministry commences two months after Haggai’s (Zech. 1:1). Work on the temple proceeds not because of a decree from Darius but because of the preaching of God’s prophets and the obedient response of God’s people (Hag. 1:14, 15).

**5:1 over them.** Both the people (Deut. 28:10) and the prophets (Jer. 15:16) belong to God.

**5:2 supporting them.** The help the prophets extend to the civil and religious leaders of the community takes the form of courageous preaching and constant encouragement (as in the books of Haggai and Zechariah).

The work that resumed under God’s direction is soon put to the test and threatened with a prohibition order by the Persian authorities (vv. 3, 4). However, in God’s providence, the people are allowed to continue until a directive is received from the emperor. The letter sent to him (5:6–17), the record of Cyrus’s decree (6:1–5), and Darius’s permission to proceed (6:6–12) are all duly recorded. There is, however, the additional and unexpected benefit of state provision for the rebuilding work and for future sacrifices.

**5:3, 4** As soon as the work on the temple resumes, the Persian officials in control of the area investigate whether the activity has been duly authorized. Large-scale construction work might be connected with the considerable political unrest throughout the empire in the early years of Darius’s reign, so the officials want to make sure the Jews are not intent on rebellion. These officials are not as hostile as those at a later date (4:7–9) and are presented as acting honorably throughout the incident., 4

His watchful and preserving oversight. This time God chooses to intervene, and the officials permit the work to continue until they hear from Darius. Here, as throughout Ezra and Nehemiah, God becomes involved through the actions of people (see 1:1 note).
When Ezra draws up this account of earlier events, he makes use of his official position in the Persian administration to access the state archives to obtain the material.

Judea is a sub-province in the Persian Empire, not an independent political state.

**prospers in their hands.** It prospers due to the care of God (v. 5), the preaching of the prophets (vv. 1, 2), and the leadership of Zerubbabel and Jeshua (v. 2).
The question underscores Judah’s lack of independence.

Tattenai’s report to the king is comprehensive and includes the reply of the Jewish leaders to the questions of the Persian officials (vv. 3, 4).

**5:11 God of heaven and earth.** A fuller form of the more frequent title “God of heaven” (1:2 note).

**a great king of Israel.** Solomon built the original temple in the years 966–959 B.C.. (1 Kin. 6:1, 38).

God used Nebuchadnezzar to punish Israel for breaking the covenant.

**Chaldean.** The Chaldeans lived in southern Mesopotamia and established the Neo-Babylonian Empire by overthrowing the Assyrians in 612 B.C.. The new empire continued until it was overthrown by the Persians in 539.
Here is the answer, on the human level, to the question posed in 5:3.

See note on 1:8. As the Persian appointee, his role is emphasized in dealing with another Persian official, even though the work has in fact been delegated to Zerubbabel (see Hag. 1:12–14; Zech. 4:9).
The work is not done continuously but experiences a break of about seventeen years (4:24 note). The Jewish elders view the work as suspended, not abandoned.

This is the second reference to an archival search, underscoring the theme of the power of written documents (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). The search mentioned earlier (4:15) stopped the building of the wall. This second search (recorded later, but occurring earlier) will result in the completion of the temple.

A search of the royal archives unearths an official copy of Cyrus’s decree, which Darius then endorses. God overrules the interference of the officials so that the work proceeds with state protection and support.

**6:1, 2** Darius responds to Tattenai’s request. The search begins in the treasury at Babylon, but the decree is found in Achmetha (Ecbatana), almost three hundred miles (480 km) northeast of Bab­ylon, and probably the city from which Cyrus issued the decree when he stayed there in the summer of 538 B.C.

**6:2 a scroll.** Probably written on leather, it is an official memorandum regarding the decree and not its exact text, which would have been preserved on a clay tablet.

This copy of the decree differs somewhat from that in 1:2–4; e.g., God’s name (“LORD”) is not used. The copy in 1:2–4 is what the heralds proclaimed to the Jews, while this copy is the minutes kept as an official record.

**6:3 Its height shall be sixty cubits and its breadth sixty cubits.** These dimensions are larger than those of Solomon’s temple (1 Kin. 6:2). They may give the maximum size allowed rather than the size planned.
Probably the layer of timber provides a measure of shock-proofing against earthquakes (see 1 Kin. 6:36; 7:12). The cost is to be met from state funds, something not mentioned in 1:2–4.
Having found Cyrus’s decree, Darius issues a second decree reinforcing it. In God’s providence, the opposition of Tattenai and his associates turns out for the good of the project (see Gen. 50:20).
Unlikely to be a reference to a member of the Persian administration; most probably Zerubbabel is in view.
As a result of the opposition, provision is also made for continuing the temple services.

verse_quote: pray for the life of the king.
note: See note on 1:3.

This decree thwarts those opposing the temple rebuilding effort, and it features the customary ancient Near Eastern curses on anyone who changes an official document (see Rev. 22:18, 19). As a result of the opposition they have faced, God’s people are granted irrevocable support to rebuild the temple.

**impaled on it.** Execution by impalement was a common Persian form of capital punishment.

verse_quote: did with all diligence what Darius the king had ordered.
note: Darius orders that his decree be carried out “with all diligence” (6:12), i.e., with care and thoroughness, and the Persian officials are careful to comply (see the diligence of the builders, 5:8).

God has worked through the leadership of the community (see 5:5). Note that there is no mention of Zerubbabel. As with his predecessor Sheshbazzar, we are never told what becomes of him.

**the prophesying of Haggai ... and Zechariah.** The preaching of the prophets moves the people to start the work again (5:1, 2) and to complete it.

**God ... Cyrus.** The same word is used for the command of God and the Persian kings’ decree, a singular form treating the edicts of the various kings as essentially one in purpose—that of God. God’s sovereign decree does not negate human responsibility but rather establishes it. The reference to Artaxerxes, who reigned in the next century, may seem out of place, since the temple proper was completed before he became king. However, the temple is not explicitly mentioned in the Aramaic text of v. 14, so the reference could be a preview to the finishing of the rebuilding of the entire “house of God,” including the community and the wall that were rebuilt under the authority of Artaxerxes (7:11–26; Neh. 2:1, 8).

Use of the name of the month may reflect Ezra’s source (see Neh. 1:1). The date corresponds to March 12, 515 B.C.., nearly four-and-a-half years after the work began in earnest (Hag. 1:15), twenty years after the restoration work was first started (3:8), and almost exactly seventy years after the Solomonic temple was destroyed in 586.

This designation focuses on their status as the covenant people of God (see v. 21).

**the dedication of this house of God.** With the solemn assignment of the completed temple for the worship of the Lord, a major milestone has been reached. The parenthetical section of 4:6–23 has already given a preview of trouble to come. The dedication of the wall (Neh. 12:27) and the final reforms (Neh. 13) will complete the restoration of the Jewish community.

The number of offerings is small in comparison to those of Solomon (1 Kin. 8:62, 63), but the reference to “12 male goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel” points to the ideal unity of the community (see 2:2; 1 Kin. 18:31). Reference to a sin offering indicates their awareness of sin and of their need for faith in God, who keeps His covenant of love (Deut. 7:9).

verse_quote: written in the Book of Moses.
note: The written text prescribes the sacred duties, and the chastened and restored community is careful to carry out all covenantal obligations. Contrary to many reconstructions of these events, this verse makes clear that the restored community had the Book of Moses in its possession long before the arrival of Ezra. The first Aramaic section of Ezra ends with this verse.
The first celebration of the Passover since the destruction of the temple seventy years earlier. The date of this Passover is April 21, 515 B.C.., a month after the completion of the temple (v. 15).

verse_quote: every one who had joined them.
note:
While this may include Gentiles (see Num. 9:14), it is more likely that the writer is referring to people of Judah (and possibly of the former northern kingdom) who were never deported and have remained in the land since the rest of the population went into exile. In large measure, they have assimilated to pagan practices, but if they repent of this and separate (a key issue for the holy people; see Introduction: Theology of Ezra), then are incorporated into the covenant community and allowed to participate in its worship.

**to worship the** LORD**.** Lit. “to seek the LORD.” They have renounced pagan practices and now seek to ascertain God’s will so that they might order the whole of their lives by it. “To seek God” is virtually a technical term for a true worshiper and diligent follower of the Lord.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread lasted throughout the week after the Passover (Lev. 23:6–8). The restored people in the rebuilt temple are once more enjoying fellowship with their God. Their joy is the Lord’s gift to them through His control of the actions of pagan kings, both Cyrus (1:1) and here Darius.

**the king of Assyria.** The reference is to Darius. The Assyrian Empire ceased to exist a century earlier, and by this time its former territory is under Persian control. Mention of Assyria probably indicates that the judgment on Israel, begun through that regime, is now reversed.

Only in these closing chapters are we introduced to Ezra, after whom the book is named. We are also permitted to read parts of his personal memoirs. These certainly include 7:27–9:15, where the “I” and “me” refer to Ezra. Since the words “such a thing” in 7:27 link back to his letter of commission in 7:12–26 this letter was likely preserved among Ezra’s personal documents as well. The remaining material in these chapters was probably added by whoever drew the source material together into the book we now have.

**7:1–10** These verses are an introductory summary of Ezra’s return to Jerusalem, about which greater detail is provided later in the chapter. Here the focus is on Ezra’s credentials and the secret of his competence as a leader.

**7:1 Now after this.** Nearly sixty years have passed between the events at the end of ch. 6 and those at the beginning of ch. 7. The only information we have on this period from Ezra and Nehemiah concerns opposition in the days of Ahasuerus (4:6 note)—the events in the book of Esther also occur during this period (Esth. 1:1).

**Artaxerxes.** Artaxerxes I, king of Persia from 465 to 424 B.C.. Some scholars have understood the reference to be to a later Artaxerxes, thus setting Ezra’s ministry many years subsequent to that of Nehemiah, but such scenarios are at variance with the scriptural account.

**Ezra.** The lengthy introduction of Ezra (vv. 1–10) signals his importance for what follows. The first information given about Ezra is his ancestry. The genealogy spanning seventeen generations is full but not complete (six more names may be added on the basis of 1 Chr. 6:3–15); the phrase “son of” is often used to mean “descendant.” Ezra’s line goes back to Aaron, establishing his priestly authority for his subsequent actions. Seraiah was high priest when Jerusalem fell (see 2:2), and so he is not Ezra’s immediate father but a more remote ancestor. Hilkiah was the high priest under Josiah (2 Kin. 22:4).

Not all the pious exiles returned with Sheshbazzar in 538 B.C.. Ezra’s family did not. Probably, Ezra was not yet born at the time of the first return. He grew up in Babylon, where most of the exiles lived.

**a scribe skilled.** In the OT, scribes were often government officials who composed official documents (4:8 note; 2 Sam. 8:17; 1 Kin. 4:3), administered temple treasuries (2 Kin. 12:10, 11; 22:3, 4, 9; Neh. 13:13), served as court emissaries (2 Kin. 18:18–37), and provided literary functions such as taking dictation (Jer. 36:32). Ezra is a high-ranking official in the Persian administration (v. 25), but his most important qualification is as a teacher of God’s law (vv. 10, 11, 14; Neh. 8:1–9).

**that the LORD ... had given.** The “Law of Moses” is divine in origin (see 2 Tim. 3:16). The reference here is to the first five books of the Bible.

**the king granted him all that he asked.** The actions of responsible human beings are traced back to the sovereign action of God: Ezra takes the initiative and asks. The content of his petition is not specified but presumably corresponds to what he was granted in his letter of commission (vv. 12–26). Artaxerxes grants his request because God providentially gives success to Ezra’s endeavor.

Ezra is not alone but is leading a second group of returning exiles.

**the seventh year.** 458 B.C..

The trip takes place in the spring, when there is ample water along the way. It takes nearly four months, from April 21 to August 4, and covers about 850 miles (1370 km), proceeding north along the banks of the Euphrates before turning south.

verse_quote: the good hand of his God.
note: Success is attributed to God’s providence. This or a similar expression occurs frequently in Ezra and Nehemiah (see 7:6, 28; 8:18, 22, 31; Neh. 2:8, 18).

Ezra’s goal in going to Jerusalem is now given. As a diligent hearer and doer of the Word (James 1:22), Ezra’s goal is to teach others to do the same.

**to study ... to do ... to teach.** Lit., “to seek.” Only here is the Hb. verb “to study” (lit. to seek”) used with “the Law” as its object. Ezra seeks to know more about God and His will (see 6:21 note) through studying His Word. Ezra is a model reformer in that he first follows God’s precepts himself (see Ps. 119:100) and then, having studied and put into practice the law, Ezra is equipped to teach others (see Ps. 51:13).

A copy of a letter from King Artaxerxes records his commission of Ezra to return to Jerusalem to inquire about the spiritual state of the people (v. 14), to provide supplies for the temple (vv. 15–24), and to arrange for the administration of justice (vv. 25, 26). Included is a specific directive to local Persian officials to provide Ezra with all that is necessary (vv. 21–23).

**7:11 letter.** The letter (vv. 12–26), written in Aramaic (4:7 note), gives Ezra the authority to carry out the reforms recorded in the following chapters. The letter may have been written by Ezra and then signed by Artaxerxes, or Artaxerxes may have had Jewish advisors help compose the letter, as some of the details seem to indicate.

A title used by Persian monarchs to indicate their supremacy over all subject kings. That God is the true King of kings is implicit in the book of Ezra (1:1 note) and explicit elsewhere in Scripture (Rev. 17:14; 19:16).

**scribe.** See note on v. 6.

This phrase describes them in their religious status as the covenant community and may well indicate Jewish input to the drafting of the letter. As in the original decree of Cyrus in 1:3, the permission to return extends to all who are willing.

This refers to the inner cabinet who had special access to the king (see Esth. 1:14), a feature of Persian administration documented by Greek historians.

**to make inquiries.** Whereas Cyrus commissioned the first returnees “to build” a temple, Artaxerxes commissions Ezra to inquire about the spiritual condition of the people. His efforts will help rebuild the community of God’s people, God’s “house” (Num. 12:7). It may be that the verb is a technical term, implying more than inquiry and having the sense “to examine” or “to superintend.”
Artaxerxes’ knowledge of the details of Israelite worship indicates that Ezra or Jewish advisors wrote the letter themselves or assisted in writing it (1:2–4 note).
Conformity to God’s will is a major theme in the rest of the book.
The generosity of Artaxerxes is like that of Darius (6:9). The amounts involved are enormous, but the Persian Empire is very wealthy.

See note on 1:3. Egypt, with Greek assistance, rebelled against Persia in 460 B.C., and the unrest was not totally suppressed at the time Ezra traveled to Jerusalem. It suits Artaxerxes to strengthen a loyal community as a buffer state.
Exemption of temple personnel from taxation is not uncommon. Again, note the indications of Jewish input in the details of temple personnel.

Ezra’s role is twofold: exercising governmental authority and teaching the law of God (7:6 note).

**all the people ... Beyond the River.** The Jews who have returned to Judah and Jerusalem. Ezra is not given authority over other nationalities.

verse_quote: the law of your God and the law of the king.
note:
The two are not identical. The distinction between religious and civil law is more important for the Jews in exile under a foreign civil power than during the monarchy, when the state was of the same religion as the people. The second Aramaic section of Ezra ends with this verse.

**let judgment be strictly executed.** Ezra himself is not given the authority to punish; the “officials and the elders” exercise it in 10:8.

Ezra reverts to Hebrew in his doxology. He expresses his joy at God’s endorsement of the enterprise.

**7:27 put such a thing ... into the heart of the king.** The actions of Artaxerxes are traced to the sovereign action of God.

verse_quote: extended to me his steadfast love.
note:
“Steadfast love” translates the Hb. word _hesed_, which refers to God’s covenant loyalty. The same word occurs in 9:9. Artaxerxes’s favor toward Ezra is due to God’s covenant loyalty to His people. “To me” is the first reference to Ezra in the first person, evidence of Ezra as the source of these “memoirs” (Introduction: Author).

**to me.** The first reference to Ezra in the first person, evidence of Ezra as the source of these “memoirs” (see Introduction: Author).

**the hand of the** LORD**.** Ezra’s awareness of God’s providential control is a source of encouragement for the tasks that lie ahead (see v. 9).

Not all the exiles returned in response to the decree of Cyrus in 538 B.C.. A second but significantly smaller group returned with Ezra about eighty years after the first return. Many of these returnees in Ezra’s day are related to those who have already gone back to Jerusalem. Allowing for the later contingent of Levites (vv. 15–20) and women and children, the second group numbers between four thousand and five thousand, about a tenth the size of the original group.

The narrative of Ezra’s return relates four matters: finding Levites prepared to return to Jerusalem (vv. 15–20); spiritual preparations for the journey (vv. 21–23); practical arrangements for transporting the valuables (vv. 24–30); and the actual journey and arrival in Jerusalem (vv. 31–36).

**8:15 the river that runs to Ahava.** Probably a canal connected to the river Euphrates, but its exact location is unknown.

**none of the sons of Levi.** Ezra wants more Levites for service in the temple (v. 17) and perhaps to help with the sacrifices mentioned in v. 35. He may also want Levites to be part of the caravan to the Promised Land—just like they were at the time of the exodus from Egypt and the first return from Babylon (1:2 note). The Levites also have responsibility for teaching the law, a task that needs to be carried out.
Ezra selects a group of influential men to persuade some Levites to return with him. Meshullam may be the same individual as in 10:15, 29.

verse_quote: the leading man at the place Casiphia.
note: The location is not certain, but it could be Ctesiphon on the river Tigris north of Babylon. Obviously there is a settlement of Levites there. However, both earlier (Deut. 12:5; Jer. 7:2, 3) and later, “the place” refers to a holy place, and it may be that Casiphia is the site of a sanctuary. There is a Jewish sanctuary at Elephantine, Egypt, at this time. Levites would be concentrated at such a sanctuary, explaining why Ezra sends the delegation to Casiphia. Iddo is probably the leader at the sanctuary, but that is not conclusively established.

verse_quote: the good hand of our God.
note: Ezra does not weary of ascribing his success to God’s providential control (7:9 note). Thirty-eight Le­vites are persuaded to return along with three key Levitical leaders and 220 temple servants (“Nethinim”). Just as the Lord stirred the spirits of Cyrus (1:1), the first returnees (1:5), and Artaxerxes (7:27), so His good hand moves these Levites to accept Ezra’s call.

Fasting is an aspect of humbling oneself for the purpose of requesting something from God (2 Chr. 20:3).

**a safe journey.** Safety from bandits, among other dangers, is in view (v. 31).

Ezra testifies to God’s providential control not only before the saints but also before Artaxerxes. It seems inconsistent with this testimony to ask for a military escort. See note on Neh. 2:7–9 for a contrast between Ezra and Nehemiah on this point.
Not then and there with words but throughout the journey with actions (vv. 31, 32).
Twelve priests and twelve Levites, perhaps as representatives of all Israel (see v. 35). Ezra is not reluctant to delegate responsibilities to others.

The total contribution listed in v. 26 is enormous, such that critics have doubted the authenticity of the list. However, the Persian kings are known for their great wealth and generosity toward the religions of subject peoples. There are also wealthy Jewish families in Babylon at this time.
For the enormous amounts involved, cf. 7:22.

LORD**.** Holiness is an attribute of God (Lev. 19:2) and, by extension, of anyone or anything belonging to Him, especially priests (Lev. 21:6), Levites (Num. 3:11–13, where “consecrated” means “dedicated” to God), and temple articles (Ex. 30:22–29). Ezra’s strict command arises from the spiritual threat that contact with the profane represents for the holy.

According to 7:9, Ezra began to gather fellow Jews and depart from Babylon on the first day. The difference is due to the delay (until April 19 458 B.C..) experienced in order to find the needed Levites.

**he delivered us.** That is, God keeps them from being attacked or ambushed rather than rescuing them after they are waylaid. Again Ezra attributes his success to God’s providential control. The fasting and prayer for a safe journey are answered with the arrival of people and possessions in Jerusalem (vv. 21, 32).
Cf. the similar rest of Nehemiah in Neh. 2:11 (see Josh. 3:2).
These temple officials may also be mentioned in Nehemiah (Neh. 3:4, 21; 11:16; 10:9, respectively).

Just as the provisions were made (7:17), so the sacrifices are offered. This is a picture of complete success. Again, the number “twelve” signifies completion (v. 24 note). The impersonal style of vv. 35, 36 probably indicates that these verses were inserted into the memoir by the compiler of the book.

So that there will be no misunderstanding, the officials in surrounding areas of the empire are informed of the royal warrant for what Ezra is about to do, A “satrap” is a ruler of a province of the empire; “governors” are high-ranking officials under a satrap.

Return to the Land of Promise is a means, not an end. The people are to aim at worshiping God and enjoying fellowship with Him. That requires adherence to God’s covenant requirements. Ezra must direct the community as to how to deal with intermarriage with surrounding peoples. The books of Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther reflect an acceptance of Persian overlordship and the need for a minority group to relate to the political authorities of their day. However, such cooperation with others cannot be at the expense of compromising their overriding loyalty to the Lord. The danger of interfaith marriages is assimilation to the surrounding culture and religion and the loss of their distinctive commitment to the Lord alone.

**9:1–15** Four-and-a-half months after arriving in Jerusalem (see 10:9), Ezra is informed about the prevalence of marriages with women of surrounding nations (vv. 1, 2). This causes him great personal distress (vv. 3–5) as a result of which he engages in confession and prayer (vv. 6–15).

**9:1 the officials approached me and said.** Ezra has come to teach the law (7:10 note) and has not adopted a confrontational approach to any irregularities he detects in the life of the community. But now some of the leaders come to him to report certain sins. Probably these leaders are not from the party who returned with Ezra but from the earlier returnees. Possibly they are responding to Ezra’s teaching, which has sensitized them to what is wrong in the land.

**have not separated themselves.** The point is the difference of religion, not race, as the following verses indicate (vv. 10–12; 4:3 note). Marriage to a foreign woman who maintains the beliefs of her people brings polytheistic worship of pagan deities into the family circle and undermines the covenant commitment of future generations.

**the peoples of the lands.** Of those listed, only the Ammonites, Moabites, and Egyptians are present in the days of Ezra. The others were in the land during the conquest under Joshua, and the mention of them could have brought to mind the original prohibitions against intermarriage (Ex. 34:10–16; Deut. 7:1–4).

**with their abominations.** Instead of “with,” it is preferable to retain “according to” or “like” in the translation. The idolatrous practices of the nations in Ezra’s day are compared to those encountered among the heathen when Israel first entered the land.

The problem is not intermarriage of different ethnic groups but the confusion of those set apart as holy by covenant with the Lord with those who are outside the covenant and therefore unclean (8:28 note; 9:11 note). “Holy race” or “holy seed” reminds the people that the Messiah will come from them.

**the officials.** The word for “officials” here is the same as in v. 1. Not all the leaders are guilty of leading people to sin; some of them are leading the way to reform.

verse_quote: I tore my garment and my cloak.
note:
A typical way of expressing grief (2 Sam. 13:19).

**pulled hair from my head and beard.** An unusual action. Some years later, Nehemiah encounters the same sin, but rather than pulling out his own hair, he pulls out the hair of the offenders (Neh. 13:25).

**sat appalled.** Sitting inactively is a natural and accepted response to overwhelming tragedy (Job 2:13). “Appalled” denotes an intense inward reaction of numbing shock because the covenant people have begun to compromise their fidelity to the Lord. It was such behavior that led to the judgment of the exile.

There is a group that has not intermarried but fears the Lord and keeps His law (see Is. 66:2).

**the evening sacrifice.** Mid-afternoon, a time of prayer as well as sacrifice (Ps. 141:2).

verse_quote: fell upon my knees and spread out my hands.
note: See 1 Kin. 8:54. Kneeling expresses humility before the majestic Lord (Ps. 95:6), and spreading the hands often accompanies petitions (Ps. 28:2). Ezra has gone to the temple, as 10:1 makes clear. For similar prayers of confession of national sin and intercession, see Neh. 1:4–11; 9:5–37; Dan. 9:3–19.

Previously, Ezra was ashamed to ask Artaxerxes for protection on the return trip (8:22). Now his shame is of a different kind, disgrace joined with the guilt that results from sin.

**our iniquities ... our guilt.** Ezra is acutely aware of the people’s sin and guilt before God. Note also the sudden shift from “my” to “our.” Though Ezra is not guilty of marrying into paganism, he identifies himself with the people in their sin, as does the Suffering Servant of Isaiah (Is. 53:12; 2 Cor. 5:21).

verse_quote: From the days of our fathers.
note: There is a sense of corporate solidarity and mutual responsibility that spans the generations of the covenant community.

The status of the returnees as the recipients of God’s favor is in jeopardy. The same word is repeated later in the verse (“brief ... a little”) to emphasize how marginal and tenuous the situation is.

**favor has been shown by the LORD ... a remnant.** Justice demands the absolute end of the people of God, but grace preserves a remnant. Through this remnant the Messiah will come, and redemption will be accomplished.

**secure hold.** The word translated “secure hold” means a stake that holds a tent in position (Judg. 4:21) or a nail that holds up objects that are hung on it (Is. 22:23–25). The Lord has given Israel a place in His temple, like the peg of a tent, and has made Ezra someone who could be trusted with burdens.

**brighten our eyes.** An idiom for increased vigor (Ps. 13:3).

Though restored to their land, the people of God are not politically independent like they were during the monarchy (4:19–23 note).

**God has not forsaken us.** God’s promise not to forsake the nation is, in its outer, typological aspect, conditional (10:5 note). If Israel forsakes God and the covenant by disregarding the law, she will forfeit the blessings and experience the curses (Deut. 28:20; 29:24, 25; 31:16, 17). Even so, God has promised never to finally desert Israel, through whom Christ comes. See Lev. 26:44, 45; Ps. 89:30–37; Is. 54:7; Rom. 11.

**the kings of Persia.** Specifically Cyrus (550–530 B.C..), who issued the decree to return; Darius (522–486 B.C.), who confirmed the decree; and Artaxerxes (465–424 B.C..), who commissioned Ezra to teach the people.

**protection in Judea and Jerusalem.** Does not refer to the wall built later by Nehemiah but instead is a figure for the protection afforded the returnees (note the figurative language in v. 8 and that the wall of Nehemiah is not built around all of Judah).
Forsaking the commandments means that covenant curses can fall upon the people at any time (v. 9 note).

Moses was the prophet who gave the command initially (Deut. 7:1–3). The words are not a quotation of a single text but a summary of the theology of separation taken from numerous texts, including Lev. 18:25; Deut. 4:5; 7:3; 18:9; 27:3; and 2 Kin. 21:16. Intermarriage with people outside the covenant introduces a relentless temptation to corrupt or abandon worship of the true and living God (see Deut. 7:3, 4; Judg. 14:1–4; 1 Kin. 11:1–4; 2 Cor. 6:14).
The restoration is on the basis of grace and the promise of the Abrahamic covenant (Deut. 4:25–31). So also was the initial entrance into the land (Deut. 9:5).

Ezra fears that the current covenant breach might result in ultimate judgment. Though judgment will later come upon the nation (Luke 20:9–19), even then there will be a remnant according to grace (Rom. 11:1–5).
Ezra’s conclusion is that even now the people live only because of God’s grace.

Ezra’s prayer is heard by the crowd gathered at the temple. Their reaction parallels that of Ezra, incorporating grief (v. 1), confession (v. 2), and repentance (vv. 3–17). One man acts as the catalyst to induce a spiritual reaction and as a channel for articulating their response.

**10:1 Ezra ... weeping.** Other leaders set the pace for sin (9:2). Now Ezra sets the pace for repentance, not by exhorting the people to mourn but by mourning himself and pricking their consciences. The bitter weeping of a substantial section of the population shows that they appreciate the gravity of the situation.

Ezra’s confession in 9:13, 14 becomes the confession of the people through one of their leaders, Shecaniah. If his father, Jehiel, is the same person listed among the sons of Elam in v. 26, Shecaniah is aware of the problem in his own family circle.

**there is hope.** Shecaniah encourages Ezra that all is not lost. In contrast to Ezra’s despair, he argues that there is still a way to recover from the existing situation.

Not an entirely new covenant but the renewal of the Mosaic covenant in terms of an oath (v. 5) to keep the stipulation regarding intermarriage (Deut. 7:3; see Jer. 34:8–22 for a similar covenant renewal).

**to put away.** This is not the usual Hb. phrase for divorce and is used only here. The Hb. expression in v. 2 (“have married ... women”) is not the usual phrase for marriage, and is used in the same way only in Neh. 13 in an analogous situation. The writer’s choice of language seems to indicate that he does not regard the unions as legitimate marriages or the sending away as actual divorce. Alternatively, the language used may indicate that this is a special situation in which divorce is preferable to the more serious transgression of allowing the holy seed (9:2) to be debased by intermarriage, thereby imperiling the people’s role as those through whom the Messiah will come.

**according to the Law.** The law does not provide explicitly for this exact situation. The phrase may refer to sending a woman and her children away along with some provisions (Gen. 21:14) and certain legal rights (Deut. 21:10–14).

As the recognized leader of the community, Ezra is responsible for formulating and coordinating their response. He is assured of the backing of the people in taking steps to renew their engagement to the covenant.

Ezra responds to the encouragement of Shecaniah and puts his advice into practice. Ezra’s action may not constitute a universal norm. He is dealing with a situation of defiance of the covenant, whereas Paul in 1 Cor. 7:12–14 is dealing with marriages entered into before conversion.

**made ... all Israel take an oath.** The covenant is conditional, as the swearing of the oath by the Israelites and not by the Lord indicates (9:9 note; Jer. 34:8–22).

Located in the temple. Jehohanan is also called “Johanan” (Neh. 12:23); he is the grandson of Eliashab.

**neither eating bread nor drinking water.** A total fast was rare (Deut. 9:18). The fast indicates that Ezra does not think the exiles are immune to the covenant punishments on the basis of an oath alone.

**the faithlessness of the exiles.** “Faithlessness,” see 9:1, 4. “The exiles” (_golah_) refers to those who have returned from exile.

Ezra was given authority to act in this way by the king (7:26), but it is not said that he issued this proclamation, which would be publicly delivered by a herald. Ezra’s preferred mode of operation (see vv. 1, 2) is to wait for others to respond to the lead he has given them by his teaching and example. Verse 8 suggests that the officials and elders take the initiative on this occasion.

Owing to the reduced territory of Judah, three days are sufficient for any who want to travel to Jerusalem.

**forfeited ... banned.** Lit. “caused to be separate” (see 9:1). Failure to comply will result in the loss of property and excommunication (7:26). If the call for separation from entanglement with those outside the community (see Introduction: Theology) goes unheeded, there will be forcible expulsion from the community.

See note on 1:5.

**the ninth month, on the twentieth day of the month.** December 19, 457 B.C., during the rainy season. At this time, Jerusalem is colder than most of the countryside around it, and rainfall in the region is more concentrated than in temperate climates.

**all the people.** The people as a whole respond to the proclamation.

**trembling because of this matter.** Ezra’s spiritual distress has spread throughout the populace (v. 1 note), though physical conditions play a part as well.

Lit. “give thanks and praise to.” When a person confesses sin and trusts in God for mercy, praise is given to God. In Ps. 103, the psalmist “blesses” God by confessing who God is and what He has done.

**do his will.** Confession must lead to repentance (v. 6 note).

**Separate yourselves.** See note on 9:11 (see Num. 16:21; 2 Cor. 6:14).
Not only do all the men assemble and express their distress (v. 9), but they also agree with Ezra as to their sin and guilt.
Not an attempt to escape the responsibility to repent but an expression of genuine concern that the repentance be carried out well.

verse_quote: with them the elders and judges of every city.
note: Local knowledge should lead to better-informed judgments as well as more rigorous supervision of the verdict.
They probably oppose the delay, though they oppose the sending away of the foreign women. Meshullam may be among those who errs in this matter (v. 29), though the name is common in this period.

It takes from “the first day of the tenth month” (December 29, 458 B.C.) until “the first day of the first month” (March 27, 457 B.C.). The problem is so widespread that the commission takes three months, not a single day (v. 13), to scrutinize all the cases. 17

Ezra carefully lists the members of the high priest’s family (v. 18) first, then other priests (vv. 20–22), then the Levites (v. 23), and finally the rest of the community (vv. 25–43). There is no cover-up of the misconduct of the influential. From this list of those guilty of intermarriage, it is evident that the individual who sins cannot find sanctuary within the larger community (Deut. 29:19–21). But for those who will avail themselves of the sacrifice provided by God, there is always forgiveness (v. 19).
